extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy of mathematics and philosophy of science (those studying mathematical explanation and models)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply criteria for when mathematical models or proofs count as explanatory (vs merely true), including representational, modal, structural, and methodological standards discussed in contemporary philosophy of mathematics and science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models need not be true to explain
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific models do not need to be true in order to explain; all that needs to occur is for the model to provide some truths by representing the right things about the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of falsehoods in a model does not preclude explanatory power so long as the model captures the explanatorily relevant features of the target; anti-pattern: rejecting a model solely because it contains idealizations or false auxiliary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional representational requirement for explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional approaches take explanation to be in virtue of an element of the model representing some explanatorily relevant factor such as a cause or non-causal difference-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether elements of the model correspond to factors that can be plausibly taken as explanatorily relevant to the target phenomenon; if not, traditional representational accounts may struggle to classify the model as explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory significance of mathematical operations between models
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical operations that connect models (e.g., limit operations) can be significant for a mathematical explanation of empirical phenomena (Batterman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an operation (such as taking a thermodynamic limit) that transforms one model into another contributes explanatory insight; example: thermodynamic limit explains universality in phase transitions even when individual models differ microscopically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealizations as operations-changing interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some idealizations function by changing or removing the interpretation of elements of the model (e.g., treating an ocean as infinitely deep or a planet as a point particle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how the idealization alters interpretation and whether this change helps generate the explanatorily relevant features; distinguish cases where idealization merely simplifies versus where it is tied to an operation that yields essential explanatory roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential nontraditional idealizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain 'mathematical idealizations' resulting from operations can be essential to the explanation without themselves representing the system(s) in question (Batterman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss idealizations as explanatorily irrelevant just because they lack a direct representational reading; evaluate whether they are essential to deriving explanatory generalizations (anti-pattern: forcing a representational reading where the explanation is operation-based).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory indispensability argument (Colyvan/Baker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Premise structure: (1) We ought to have ontological commitment to entities indispensable to our best scientific theories; (2) Mathematical entities are indispensable to our best scientific theories; therefore (3) we ought to believe in mathematical entities. Baker's reformulation centers indispensability of explanatory role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing ontological commitments, distinguish general indispensability for theory formulation from indispensability for explanation specifically; evaluate cases (e.g., cicada prime periods) for whether mathematical entities play the same explanatory role as theoretical unobservables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circularity / presupposition worry for indispensability
rubrics_metrics.description: Steiner/Morgenbesser worry: explanatory arguments for mathematical entities may be circular because many targets presuppose mathematical notions, making comparison with non-mathematical explanations impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the explanandum itself requires mathematical characterization, which would block the comparative inferential move required by the indispensability argument; anti-pattern: treating presuppositions as neutral background rather than potentially question-begging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominalist / weak-mathematical-target worry (Pincock)
rubrics_metrics.description: If targets are characterized in weak mathematical terms, only weak mathematical theories may be needed to explain them, and these can admit nominalistic reinterpretations preserving explanatory power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze strength of mathematical resources required by an explanation; if a nominalistic re-interpretation can recover explanatory claims, the claim of indispensability is weakened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation-only account objection (Saatsi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics may only explain by representing some non-mathematical features of the physical world, so explanations need not invoke mathematical objects per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish explanations that require commitment to distinctively mathematical entities from those that merely use mathematics representationally; this challenges premise that math entails ontological commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictionalist challenge to indispensability (Leng, Yablo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical fictionalists accept distinctively mathematical explanations but argue they do not presuppose mathematical objects; modal or interpretive readings suffice for explanatory work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider fictionalist reconstruals that replace ontological commitment with modal or interpretive devices; evaluating indispensability requires showing these reconstruals fail to capture explanatory utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colyvan's 'challenge to recast' strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Colyvan challenges critics to recast mathematical explanations in non-mathematical terms; refusal is an 'easy road' to nominalism—if explanation-bearing language cannot be rendered literally, math may be indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt constructive non-mathematical reformulations of contested explanations; success undermines indispensability claims, failure supports them; anti-pattern: asserting recasting impossible without attempting constructive reformulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field's intrinsic vs extrinsic explanation standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Field argues mathematical explanations are extrinsic and that for every extrinsic explanation there is a superior intrinsic (non-mathematical) explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe whether the mathematical explanation is merely extrinsic (gives structure but not intrinsic reasons) and whether a superior intrinsic account exists; example: check intrinsic explanatory virtues rather than surface derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean structuralist defence (Baron)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some defenders claim structural properties shared by abstract and concrete systems make mathematical entities indispensable because intrinsic properties of abstract objects are also possessed by concrete entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether explanatorily relevant structural properties plausibly require reference to abstract objects (Baron's claim) or can be captured without ontological commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian realist account (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics concerns mathematical properties possessed by physical systems; these properties (not abstract objects) explain physical modal features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether treating mathematical aspects as properties immanent in physical systems preserves explanatory role while avoiding abstract objects; compare explanatory import with Pythagorean view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal mathematical explanation: explanatory proofs in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Within mathematics, explanatory activity often aims not merely to prove that a theorem is true but to show why it is true; such proofs are called explanatory or internal mathematical explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical proofs, ask whether they provide reasons/grounds that illuminate why the theorem holds (beyond establishing truth); look to cases where mathematicians reprove results for explanatory payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual grounding as target of explanatory proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory proofs track conceptual grounding (reasons/grounds why a theorem is true), not to be conflated with metaphysical grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge proofs by their ability to reveal conceptual dependencies or reasons (grounds) for the result; prefer proofs that make these grounds explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian distinction: demonstration of fact vs demonstration of reasoned fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguished demonstrations 'of the fact' (establishing truth) from demonstrations 'of the reasoned fact' (which provide explanations); only the latter are explanatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this distinction: evaluate whether a demonstration merely establishes truth or whether it identifies the 'cause' or reason that makes the fact obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity criterion for explanatory proofs (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity: a proof of a simple result should 'exploit some similar, simple feature of the setup.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs that reduce the result to a simple, salient feature in the problem setup; anti-pattern: proofs that achieve the result via heavy machinery without revealing the simple feature responsible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry criterion for explanatory proofs (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetry: when a theorem displays striking symmetry, an explanatory proof should show how that symmetry follows from a corresponding symmetry in the setup (e.g., d'Alembert's theorem explained by invariance under i↦-i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For symmetric results, check whether the proof exposes the structural symmetry in premises/setup that accounts for the result; algebraic manipulations that do not reveal this are less explanatory (Brumfiel's critique of transcendental proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory status of induction is contested
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate exists over whether proofs by induction are explanatory: Lange argues they are not (on asymmetry grounds), others defend the explanatory value of induction (Baldwin, Lehet), pointing to inductive definitions or asymmetry criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing inductive proofs, consider whether they respect explanatory asymmetry and whether they identify grounds that render the result intelligible (not merely derivational equivalence to other forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrammatic and analogical proofs as explanatory modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that explain by using diagrams or by drawing on analogies can be explanatory in distinct ways (e.g., diagram-based explanations, analogical reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate non-syntactic proofs (diagrams, analogies) for their capacity to reveal reasons/grounds; do not dismiss such proofs merely because they are non-algebraic or non-formal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological approaches: bottom-up vs top-down
rubrics_metrics.description: Two research strategies: bottom-up taxonomies (identify recurring explanatory-proof types without committing to a single theory) vs top-down general models (start with a general model and fit practice to it, e.g., Kitcher's unificationist theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate method for analysis: use bottom-up if focusing on practice and diversity of explanatory proofs; use top-down to test general theories of explanation against case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Externalist vs internalist frameworks for mathematical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Externalist (ontic) accounts look for objective dependence relations that explanations track; internalist (epistemic) accounts treat explanations as activities internal to an epistemic corpus (theory or proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether evaluation focuses on objective ontic relations (externalist criteria) or on epistemic virtues internal to mathematical practice (internalist criteria); different cases may favour different frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner's program: characterizing explanatory proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Steiner's account is an externalist attempt to find criteria that characterize explanatory proofs (mentioned as a leading contemporary externalist model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider Steiner-style criteria when seeking objective structure in how mathematical derivations yield explanations; compare with counterfactual and other externalist proposals.
